section_title: When Great Privilege Brings Greater Responsibility

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 20 Then Jesus began to denounce the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent. 21 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. 22 But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

23 And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day. 24 But I tell you that it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

context_lines: Jesus now addresses towns where much of His miraculous work has taken place. Matthew gives the reason for the rebuke: they have not repented. Seeing wonderful things has not led them to turn back to God.

The Greek word is μετανοέω, *metanoeō* (meh-tah-noh-EH-oh), to repent or change one's mind. [Thayer's entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/3340.htm) includes turning from past sins and seeking God's pardon, and specifically lists these verses. In this setting, repentance means more than being impressed by a miracle or feeling briefly sorry. It calls for a changed response to God.

The comparison with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom is deliberately startling. Jesus says those places would have responded differently if they had witnessed the works these towns received. Sackcloth and ashes describe the serious response He says would have followed. Familiarity with His works gives His hearers responsibility, rather than grounds for confidence that they are already safe.

Capernaum receives its own warning about being brought down. The contrast between being lifted to heaven and going down to Hades overturns any expectation of honor based on privilege alone. Jesus repeatedly places the comparison on the day of judgment: these towns must answer for the response they have made to the light they received.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand the passage as a warning that greater knowledge of God's work brings greater responsibility. [Wesley on Matthew 11:21–24](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) treats the woes as solemn declarations of coming misery and the comparisons as differences in the severity of judgment. The Reformed [Westminster Confession, 33.1–3](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), likewise teaches a coming judgment through Christ in which people give account, and presents that certainty as a reason to turn from sin and remain watchful.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The warning belongs to God's larger purpose of bringing people to repentance and judging with justice. In [Acts 17:30–31](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/17.htm), Paul announces that God calls people everywhere to repent and has appointed the risen Jesus to judge the world. Judgment is part of the good news's serious claim on human life, alongside the offer of mercy.

Jesus states the principle of responsibility more explicitly in [Luke 12:47–48](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/12.htm): the servant who knows more is answerable for more. This is a parallel teaching, not a scale by which readers can calculate another person's punishment. God's judgment takes account of what has been entrusted to people and how they respond.
